analysis.one_liner: Ends tax breaks that let U.S. companies avoid tax on profits shifted abroad.
analysis.headline: The bill had 129 cosponsors, all Democrats, but never received a committee vote or a floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise taxes on U.S.-based multinational companies' foreign profits. It requires companies to pay U.S. tax on those profits in the year earned, at the full corporate rate, and stops them from using taxes paid in one country to shield profits parked in another. It also cracks down on companies that move their headquarters overseas on paper while staying run from the U.S., and limits interest deductions used to shrink taxable income.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit indirectly: the changes raise federal revenue from large companies that now pay little U.S. tax on foreign profits, reducing pressure to cut public programs or shift taxes onto individuals. Domestic-only businesses that compete with offshore-shifting multinationals also gain a more level playing field.

how_it_helps.text: Requires U.S. shareholders to include their foreign subsidiaries' profits in the current tax year at full rates, repealing both the reduced rate on foreign intangible income and the deduction that lowered it [S2] [S3].

Applies the foreign tax credit limit country by country, so taxes paid in a low-tax haven can no longer offset profits earned in high-tax countries — a mechanism that currently shields income shifted offshore [S2] [S3].
Limits interest deductions for U.S. members of multinational groups, curbing the practice of loading U.S. operations with debt to erase taxable income [S2] [S3].

Treats more inverted corporations — companies that acquired a foreign firm to reincorporate in a low-tax country — as domestic for tax purposes, and taxes foreign corporations managed and controlled primarily in the U.S. as domestic [S2] [S3].
Taxes foreign base company oil-related income as immediately taxable income, closing a long-standing break for oil and gas multinationals [S3].

analysis.who_pays: U.S. multinational corporations and their shareholders, who would owe more U.S. tax on foreign profits. Some cost may trickle to consumers or workers, and opponents argue U.S.-headquartered firms competing abroad would face higher taxes than foreign rivals.

drawbacks.text: The country-by-country credit rule and full-rate taxation raise the U.S. tax burden on American-headquartered companies competing worldwide, which supporters of the current rules argue puts them at a disadvantage against foreign-based rivals; the higher tax may partly show up as lower wages, investment, or higher prices [S3].

The interest-deduction limit reaches any company in a group with over $100 million in gross receipts that files consolidated financial statements, adding substantial compliance complexity, and several provisions apply retroactively to tax years beginning after December 31, 2020 [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real and well-documented imbalance: multinationals can currently shrink U.S. tax on foreign profits through timing rules, blended credits, and interest shifting, while domestic-only businesses cannot. The cost is a heavier tax and compliance load on U.S.-headquartered multinationals, some of which could be passed through to workers and consumers, and the retroactive effective dates are aggressive. On balance the provisions close genuine avoidance channels rather than simply raising rates on ordinary business income.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, so it died quietly when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lloyd Doggett introduced the bill on March 11, 2021, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S5].
The bill attracted 129 cosponsors, all of them Democrats [S4].
No further action appears in the record: the committee never held a markup or vote, and the House never voted on the bill before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: U.S. multinational corporations are better off: they keep the current tax treatment of foreign profits because the bill never advanced. Some supporters hoped the ideas would be folded into a broader tax bill, but this bill itself never moved.

for.name: Lloyd Doggett
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and organized the bill's introduction with a large group of colleagues.

for.name: 129 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; no markup, no vote, no report ever appeared in the action history.

against.name: Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of jurisdiction, never scheduled the bill for consideration during the 117th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 129 cosponsors were Democrats, and with no Republican support and no recorded votes, the bill's support was entirely one-party; it never got far enough to test whether any Republicans would back it on the floor.

industries.note: They would pay U.S. tax on foreign subsidiary profits in the year earned at full rates and lose credit-blending and interest-deduction strategies that minimize U.S. tax. Their savings under current rules come at the cost of federal revenue that ordinary taxpayers otherwise must make up.
The bill makes foreign base company oil-related income immediately taxable instead of deferrable, closing a decades-old break specific to the industry.

industries.industry: Corporations that relocated headquarters abroad on paper (corporate inversions)
industries.note: Tighter inversion rules would tax more paper relocations as domestic companies, ending the tax advantage of keeping the legal address offshore while managing the business from the U.S.
